description:
We're Earth Intruders, in-person team from Dhaka, Bangladesh, taking part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We're curious about space, love solving problems, and believe great discoveries can come from anyone, anywhere.

OPEN FOR MEMBERS
summary:
NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the whole sky again and again in 102 colours of infrared light. Some things in those photos change: a rock moves, a star brightens or dims, a light appears or goes missing. There are too many photos for scientists to check by eye, so changes can go unnoticed.

BlinkSky makes that search a game anyone can play on a phone. You flip between real SPHEREx photos of the same piece of sky and tap anything that looks different. The app then checks for camera faults, compares your catch with NASA JPL's lists of known asteroids and comets, JPL Horizons and the Gaia star list, and sorts it into moved, appeared or vanished.

Every catch becomes a card with the real image and facts. Play your cards against a friend or the computer: each card's real size, speed and rarity decide who wins, so catching rarer objects makes your deck stronger.

If your catch is on no list, you can send it to our team with a draft report for the Minor Planet Center, the Transient Name Server or the AAVSO Variable Star Index. These are candidates, not discoveries, until experts confirm them.

BlinkSky also has the Explorer the challenge asks for: type any sky coordinates or pick a test object and watch a short video of how that spot changed.

Using only SPHEREx photos, we measured Barnard's Star moving 9.9 ± 0.6 arcseconds a year. Gaia's value is 10.39.
details:
BlinkSky is a web game for a phone or laptop. It shows you real SPHEREx photos of the same piece of sky, taken at different times, and flips between them. Most dots stay put. You tap the one that doesn't.

What it does

After you tap, the app does the checks a trained volunteer would normally do by hand:

1. If SPHEREx took another photo a few minutes later, it looks there too. A real light shows up in both, a camera fault in only one. If there is no extra photo, the card says it needs a second sighting.

2. It asks NASA JPL whether a known asteroid or comet was at that spot at that time.

3. It checks the Gaia star list, in case it is a known star.

4. It sorts the change: moved, appeared, or vanished.

5. For a known object, it compares where you saw it with where NASA's orbit says it should be.

A known object becomes a card in your deck, with the real SPHEREx image, its size, speed, distance and its colour fingerprint (how bright it is in each of SPHEREx's colours). You can play your cards against the computer, or send a friend a challenge link.

If the change is on no list, the card is saved as a new find. From your deck you can send it to our team: the app opens an email with a dated receipt and a draft report in the format the official lists use. That is the Minor Planet Center for things that move, the Transient Name Server for new lights, and the AAVSO Variable Star Index for lights that go out. Our team checks it before anything goes further. We call these candidates, not discoveries, and so far we have not reported any.

BlinkSky also has the Explorer the challenge asks for. Type any sky coordinates, or pick one of the five test objects (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis). It fetches the SPHEREx photos live, which takes about a minute for a new spot, and plays them as a short video. You can switch colour bands, add frames together, subtract them, stack all visits, change the field of view, turn on Gaia and WISE markers, open the same spot in Aladin, and share the view as a link.

Benefits and impact

SPHEREx photographs the whole sky again and again, and no team of scientists can look at all of it by eye. Citizen science programs already let volunteers help, but a volunteer has to learn special software and do many checks by hand. That stops a lot of people.

BlinkSky leaves the fun part to the player, which is spotting the change, and lets the code do the rest. A school student with a phone can do with a tap what used to take training. If thousands of people play, thousands of eyes go over photos nobody would otherwise have looked at, and only finds that pass the checks and our own review go any further.

It teaches too. Every card is a real object with real facts, and the Explorer lets you watch a star actually move across the sky in about a year of photos.

We wanted to know if our measurements can be trusted, so we measured how fast Barnard's Star moves using only SPHEREx photos. We got 9.94 ± 0.56 arcseconds per year. Gaia says 10.39, so we are within 5 percent. For Epsilon Indi B we got 4.54 ± 0.19, and Gaia says 4.68.

Tools we used

The game is a single web page in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. There is no framework and no login, and it is hosted free on GitHub Pages.

Python with Astropy prepares the game rounds from the original SPHEREx files. It cleans flagged pixels, lines the photos up, and works out sky positions.

A small Cloudflare Worker passes requests from the page to NASA's IRSA archive. That is what makes typed coordinates work live in the browser.

Aladin Lite shows the SPHEREx all-sky map, and a small QR code library makes the friend challenge codes.

Data: SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 from NASA IRSA, JPL Small-Body Identification, JPL Small-Body Database, JPL Horizons, NASA NeoWs, AllWISE, and ESA Gaia DR3.

How it is creative

A tool for this challenge is usually a viewer: you look at how a spot changes. We turned the looking into a hunt, and each result into something you keep. Your deck is a record of real objects you found yourself in NASA photos.

It also goes a step past a viewer. A catch that is on no list doesn't end as a screenshot. It ends as a dated receipt and a draft report, ready for the people who keep the official lists.

The idea comes from our own experience. Our team lead took part in an asteroid search campaign where volunteers blink telescope photos by hand. BlinkSky is that same job, made simple enough for anyone.

What we considered

The player has to do the real finding. Before you tap, a moving object looks like every star around it. A hint only narrows the area, and the card records that a hint was used.

Honesty. Card images are real SPHEREx pixels, even when they are blurry, and a new find stays a candidate until experts confirm it.

It should not feel like a gambling app, so there are no loot boxes and no flashing rewards. We redesigned the look twice for this reason.

It has to work on a cheap phone. There is nothing to install and no account, and a tap snaps to the nearest light so small screens still work.

Plain words. A 12 year old should be able to play without knowing any astronomy.
